title: The Two Shocks Upending Latin America
gist: Restrepo and Zuniga argue Latin America faces twin external shocks — the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a potentially record El Niño — that are reigniting inflation, draining fiscal space and eroding support for security-focused populist leaders like Kast, Noboa and Milei. They see winners (Guyana, Argentina, Brazil, copper/gold exporters) and losers (fuel-importing Central America and the Caribbean), and urge regional integration plus EU/US-backed investment to avoid a new cycle of economic populism.

themes.theme: Voter swings driven by performance, not ideology

insights.claim: The wave of crime-focused populists elected across Latin America is not evidence of a durable rightward shift; voters are punishing traditional politicians for failing to solve everyday problems, and the next cycle may turn on rising costs and inequality.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Investors pricing a structural pro-market/right turn in the region risk being wrong-footed as cost-of-living pressures swing electorates back toward economic populists.
insights.quote: there is little evidence of a durable shift in that direction
insights.locator: Across Latin America and the Caribbean

insights.claim: Chilean President José Antonio Kast's approval fell 14 points in March 2026 after he declined to issue consumer subsidies to cushion higher energy prices.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Fiscal discipline in the face of an energy shock carries immediate political cost, raising pressure on governments to subsidize and widen deficits.
insights.locator: SHOCK WAVES FROM HORMUZ

insights.claim: Argentine President Javier Milei's disapproval rating spiked to 63% in late April from 49% at the start of the year as higher energy costs renewed inflation concerns, leaving him an uphill 2027 reelection bid despite macroeconomic improvements.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Political risk premium on Argentine assets may rise into 2027 as Milei's reform program loses popular backing.
insights.locator: SHOCK WAVES FROM HORMUZ

insights.claim: Peru's sharpest monthly inflation spike in more than 30 years helped leftist Roberto Sánchez surge unexpectedly in the April first round before narrowly losing the runoff to Keiko Fujimori.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Illustrates how quickly inflation shocks can bring anti-establishment candidates to the brink of power in the region.
insights.locator: SHOCK WAVES FROM HORMUZ

themes.theme: Hormuz closure: energy winners and losers

insights.claim: Because the region depends on imported gasoline and diesel, the prolonged effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz is imposing a growing economic toll; the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua and several Caribbean states are subsidizing energy at rising cost while others cannot afford relief.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Fuel-importing small economies face deteriorating fiscal balances and sovereign credit stress the longer oil stays high.
insights.locator: Given the region’s dependence on imported gasoline

insights.claim: The price of maize rose more than 60% in Honduras from 2025 to 2026, and soaring gasoline prices triggered public protests in Guatemala.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Food and fuel inflation in Central America is a leading indicator of social unrest and political instability.
insights.locator: Given the region’s dependence on imported gasoline

insights.claim: Guyana's oil revenues have grown more than 50% so far in 2026, making it the chief regional beneficiary of energy-market turbulence; Venezuela has also profited, though its sector's long-term viability is doubtful without a democratic transition.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Energy exporters in the region are fiscal winners of the Gulf conflict, while Venezuela's upside remains capped by political risk.
insights.locator: To be sure, some countries have benefited

insights.claim: The Trump administration's deal with Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodríguez faces congressional scrutiny that will intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the U.S. midterms.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: U.S. midterm outcomes are a swing factor for Venezuelan oil access and related investments.
insights.locator: To be sure, some countries have benefited

insights.claim: Expanding shale oil and gas has turned Argentina from a net energy importer into an exporter, Brazil has become Latin America's largest oil producer and a global top-ten producer with room to grow, and Peru and Chile are offsetting higher energy costs with copper and gold exports at record prices.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Commodity exporters—shale Argentina, Brazilian oil, Andean copper/gold—are relatively insulated; relative-value positioning favors them over fuel importers.
insights.locator: To be sure, some countries have benefited

insights.claim: If the strait remains closed, and particularly if the United States curtails diesel exports, the region will face higher energy import costs that weigh on agricultural production and drive inflation.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: A U.S. diesel export curb would be a key escalation trigger for Latin American inflation and agricultural output.
insights.quote: particularly if the United States curtails diesel fuel exports
insights.locator: Still, if the strait remains closed

insights.claim: A potentially record El Niño is likely to bring flooding to Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru, drought to Central America and the Amazon, and disruptions to key Pacific fisheries, hitting governments whose budgets were already drained by the Gulf energy shock.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Agricultural, fisheries and sovereign-fiscal risks are correlated across the region in the coming months.
insights.quote: many governments will meet these new challenges with empty coffers
insights.locator: FROM BAD TO WORSE

insights.claim: Colombia, hit by a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in August, faces El Niño pressure on its hydroelectric plants and coffee output, a major export earner.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Coffee supply and Colombian power prices are exposed to El Niño drought risk.
insights.locator: The region is already feeling some of the effects

insights.claim: Central American governments will likely have to suspend fuel taxes, forgoing substantial revenue, to head off protests; with migration to the U.S. now largely closed off, El Niño-driven farm losses are more likely to produce unrest at home rather than an outflow of migrants.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Closing the migration relief valve shifts climate-driven stress into domestic instability and fiscal erosion in Central America.
insights.locator: As Central America faces the possibility

insights.claim: Lower rainfall is reducing Panama Canal water levels and slowing shipping, further straining an already disrupted LNG trade.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Canal draft restrictions add a second chokepoint to LNG logistics alongside Hormuz, supporting freight and LNG price volatility.
insights.locator: As Central America faces the possibility

insights.claim: In Brazil, El Niño threatens soy and corn harvests and will likely strain hydropower, forcing greater reliance on costlier gas, diesel and coal generation that could require consumer subsidies and slow the country's data-center boom — all during a polarizing Lula vs. Flávio Bolsonaro election.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Brazilian power prices, ag exports and data-center buildout are vulnerable; a second-order hit to AI infrastructure investment in Brazil.
insights.locator: Given its expanse and varied climates

insights.claim: Milei's plan depends on a strong grain harvest to rebuild dollar reserves; El Niño rains could help after drought, but too much rain could damage infrastructure and yields, cutting export income and lifting food prices to the benefit of Peronist challengers in 2027.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Argentina's reserve rebuild and 2027 election odds hinge on harvest weather—a binary risk for Argentine sovereign debt.
insights.locator: In Argentina, Milei’s economic plan depends

insights.claim: Latin America and the Caribbean trade less with themselves than any other region in the world; the authors argue deeper integration, rule of law and fiscal discipline, backed by multilateral lenders like the IDB and CAF, are the path to resilience.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
entities: CAF-Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean
insights.so_what: Shared infrastructure and intraregional trade initiatives financed by MDBs are the investable policy response the authors expect/advocate.
insights.quote: No region in the world trades less with itself than Latin America and the Caribbean.
insights.locator: FULL-COURT PRESS

insights.claim: If governments fail to address inflation and food insecurity, security-focused leaders like Bukele and Noboa will harden their rhetoric, Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella may stoke xenophobia, and Kirchnerista-style economic populists will gain ground with deficit-expanding policies.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: Rising risk of fiscal deterioration and policy unpredictability across multiple Latin American sovereigns.
insights.locator: If governments in the region fail

insights.claim: The EU is positioning itself as a predictable alternative to China and the U.S.; if its Court of Justice upholds the EU-Mercosur agreement next year, free trade with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay will be locked in, alongside more than $50 billion in Global Gateway investments.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: An EU court ruling in 2027 is a catalyst for Mercosur trade flows and European investment in the region.
insights.locator: Beyond the region’s own governments

insights.claim: The Trump administration's coercion via tariffs and force may enable short-term resource grabs like Venezuela but risks squandering long-term U.S. influence; if the U.S. and Europe fail to support integration, China will deepen ties by offering quick, visible wins to governments of all stripes.
insights.speaker: Dan Restrepo
insights.so_what: U.S. coercive policy could cede critical-minerals and supply-chain influence in the hemisphere to China.
insights.quote: Quick wins will not fix the structural flaws holding back growth.
insights.locator: The United States under President Donald Trump
